set.statement: In laboratory tests of urine fentanyl test strips used on dissolved drug and read by trained staff, compared with laboratory analysis (GC/MS) of the same samples or with the known content of prepared solutions, the strips showed fentanyl in almost every sample that contained it, down to very low concentrations, but the lowest concentration they detected differed widely between studies, brands, production lots and reading rules. In 106 police-seized samples that earlier GC/MS had found to contain fentanyl (two US forensic laboratories, 2017), one brand (BTNX Rapid Response) read positive in 104 (52 of 52 in one laboratory, 52 of 54 in the other; 98 in 100, editors' Wilson 95% CI 93.4–99.5%); both samples it missed contained fentanyl alone. Because the forensic GC/MS methods were less sensitive than the strip (3.1 and 100 µg/mL), only samples with enough fentanyl for GC/MS to find could enter this positive group, so how often strips miss samples with very little fentanyl was not measured (Green et al., 2020). Second-hand figures, relayed without their conditions, mostly point the same way: in British Columbia drug-checking data, 4 of 173 fentanyl-positive samples were missed, all with fentanyl at 5% by weight or less (McCrae et al., 2020, as cited by Halifax et al., 2024); a scoping review relays sensitivity of about 96 to 98 in 100 from that study and one validation study (Kutscher et al., 2024); and another paper relays 87.5 in 100 from a validation study (Ti et al., 2020, as cited by Klaire et al., 2022). In pure fentanyl solutions, the lowest concentration detected was 100 to 150 ng/mL (Green et al., standards prepared in ethanol); 25 ng/mL by eye with five strips per concentration, counting a faint test band as positive (the pictured strips at 25 and 50 ng/mL show a faint band, which the makers' rule, any visible band means negative, reads as negative; Lockwood et al., 2021); positive at 100 ng/mL on all four brands in the main table, two of them with only a barely visible test band that the makers' rule reads as negative, and, in a descending series pictured for two brands, down to 50 and 25 ng/mL by the authors' rule (100 and 50 ng/mL by the makers' rule), with no replicates reported and one brand graded differently at 100 ng/mL in the table and the figure (Bergh et al., 2021); 20 ng/mL for two lots obtained in 2017 against 200 ng/mL for three lots obtained in 2021 (Halifax et al., 2024, duplicate strips); and 500 ng/mL for strips whose listed cut-off was 200 ng/mL, from a heat sub-study only (Sisco et al., 2024b): a 25-fold range overall (editors' calculation). The seized samples were selected on known content and tested as powders by chemists blind to it, nearly all data come from one brand, and none of these studies measured how people prepare and read strips at home. Certainty: low. Status: replicated.
set.plain: In laboratory tests, fentanyl test strips showed fentanyl in almost all drug samples that contained it: 104 of 106 police-seized samples in one study. All those samples had enough fentanyl for the laboratory's own machine to find it; samples with very little fentanyl were not tested this way. Strips can pick up very small amounts, but the smallest amount they found differed up to 25 times between studies and batches of strips, and also depended on whether a faint line was counted. Trained staff did these tests, mostly with one brand; how well strips work when people test at home was not measured.
set.magnitude: Seized samples (Green et al., 2020): sensitivity 100.0% (52/52) and 96.3% (52/54) at the two laboratories; 104/106 = 98.1% pooled (Wilson 95% CI 93.4–99.5%, editors' calculation); reference GC/MS limits 3.1 and 100 µg/mL. Lowest concentration detected in pure fentanyl solutions: 0.100–0.150 mcg/mL, that is 100–150 ng/mL (Green et al., standards in ethanol); 25 ng/mL by eye, counting a faint band (Lockwood et al., 2021); positive at 100 ng/mL on four brands, two with a barely visible band only, and in a pictured series down to 50 ng/mL (Rapid Response) and 25 ng/mL (One Step) by the authors' rule, 100 and 50 ng/mL by the makers' rule (Bergh et al., 2021); 20 ng/mL for 2017 lots and 200 ng/mL for 2021 lots (Halifax et al., 2024); 500 ng/mL, listed cut-off 200 ng/mL, heat sub-study only (Sisco et al., 2024b). Second-hand: 4 of 173 fentanyl-positive drug-checking samples missed (McCrae et al., 2020, via Halifax et al.); sensitivity about 96.3–98% (via Kutscher et al., 2024); 87.5% (Ti et al., 2020, via Klaire et al., 2022).
set.grade.domains.risk_of_bias.note: Every laboratory study is at high risk of bias by QUADAS-2 (study cards): Green et al. selected samples on known GC/MS status (106 with and 104 without fentanyl) and used a reference less sensitive than the strip, so samples with little fentanyl could not enter the positive group; Bergh et al. graded bands after seeing them, with readers not described as blind; Halifax et al. tested old and new lots in different rounds; Lockwood et al.'s limit counts a faint band that its own stated reading rule calls negative. These problems bear on specificity, on borderline readings and on sensitivity for samples with little fentanyl; counted once.
set.grade.domains.inconsistency.note: Sensitivity on real samples comes from one study (Green et al.) and agrees with second-hand drug-checking data (4 of 173 missed); a lower second-hand figure (87.5 in 100) comes without its conditions and is not counted. Detection limits span 25-fold (20 to 500 ng/mL); the claim states the range, and part of it follows lot, brand and reading rule (Halifax et al.; Bergh et al.; Lockwood et al.), so it is not rated down again.
set.grade.domains.indirectness.note: Trained laboratory staff, pure fentanyl in water or ethanol or seized samples tested as powders, mostly one brand; people ask how strips work on their own drugs at home.
set.grade.domains.imprecision.note: 104 of 106 (95% CI 93.4–99.5%); detection limits from replicated strips in most studies (triplicates, Green et al. and Sisco et al., 2024b; five strips per level, Lockwood et al.; duplicates on five lots, Halifax et al.); no replicates are reported in Bergh et al.
set.grade.reasoning: Test-accuracy evidence that compares the strip with a reference method starts high (METHODS §6.3, test accuracy); one level each for risk of bias and indirectness gives low. Rated as worded: laboratory detection of fentanyl in seized samples with enough fentanyl for GC/MS and in pure solutions, not home use and not effects on behaviour or overdose, which are separate questions. Status replicated: independent teams in five laboratories (Green et al.; Lockwood et al.; Bergh et al.; Halifax et al.; Sisco et al., 2024b) detected fentanyl at ng/mL concentrations; only Green et al. measured sensitivity on seized samples. Overlap: the review's sensitivity range comes from a study sharing authors with Green et al. and from the drug-checking data cited by Halifax et al., so it is not counted separately, and the figure relayed by Klaire et al. is second-hand and not counted. Sisco et al. (2024b) is re-filed as test-accuracy with QUADAS-2 in this round (card sc_sisco_2024b) and adds one detection limit, from its heat sub-study.

set.statement: In laboratory tests of urine fentanyl test strips on dissolved samples that contained no fentanyl, compared with laboratory analysis or known content, strips sometimes read positive, mostly with strong solutions of a few other drugs. Among 104 police-seized samples without fentanyl by earlier GC/MS, one brand (BTNX Rapid Response) read positive in 6 (1 of 52 in one laboratory, 5 of 52 in the other; specificity 94.2%, editors' Wilson 95% CI 88.0–97.3%, so about 6 in 100 read falsely positive); the five described held only buprenorphine, heroin (two), methamphetamine or noscapine, and because the GC/MS methods were less sensitive than the strip, some may have held traces of fentanyl or of a fentanyl analogue that the GC/MS methods did not find (Green et al., 2020). In solutions made in the laboratory, strong concentrations of four substances turned the strip positive with no fentanyl present: methamphetamine, MDMA, diphenhydramine and lidocaine. With one strip per concentration, solutions of one seized methamphetamine sample, one seized MDMA sample and retail diphenhydramine tablets and capsules read positive by eye above about 2 mg/mL of material and, by image analysis, from 1 to 2.5 mg/mL, while seized cocaine and alprazolam, gabapentin and buprenorphine-naloxone products read negative up to 20 mg/mL (Lockwood et al., 2021). With pure standards and duplicate strips on five lots, the thresholds for lots obtained in 2017 and in 2021 were 5 and 10 mg/mL for d-methamphetamine, 50 and 2.5–5 mg/mL for MDMA and 100 and 2.5 mg/mL for lidocaine; diphenhydramine read positive from 0.5–1 mg/mL on the 2021 lots but, unexpectedly, negative or invalid at 50 mg/mL and negative on two of three lots at 100 mg/mL, while the 2017 lots, positive at 100 mg/mL, were not tested below 50 mg/mL; l-methamphetamine (25 mg/mL), cocaine and ketamine (25 mg/mL) and levamisole (up to 100 mg/mL) did not react (Halifax et al., 2024). Twelve other drugs, among them amphetamine, cocaine, heroin, MDMA and methamphetamine, gave no false positive on four brands at 100 or 1000 ng/mL, far below the concentrations that gave false positives elsewhere, and ascorbic acid (vitamin C) at 10 mg/mL or more did so on one brand only (Bergh et al., 2021). Within the same strips, the lowest concentration that gave a false positive was 2,500 times (Halifax et al., lots obtained in 2021: 0.5 mg/mL against a fentanyl limit of 200 ng/mL) to about 40,000 times (Lockwood et al.: 1 mg/mL of material against 25 ng/mL) the lowest fentanyl concentration detected (editors' calculation). Second-hand, from validation studies and drug-checking data not read here and relayed without their conditions, specificity was about 89 in 100 (Kutscher et al., 2024) and 95 in 100 (Ti et al., 2020, as cited by Klaire et al., 2022). Outside the laboratory, people using take-home strips reported fentanyl in 73 of 265 crystal methamphetamine samples and 16 of 93 cocaine samples, against 5 of 97 and 1 of 92 other samples tested on site by staff, which the authors attribute mostly to false positives from how samples were prepared (Klaire et al., 2022; different samples, nothing confirmed, not tested). A scoping review lists cocaine, gabapentin, alprazolam and buprenorphine-naloxone among causes of false positives, citing Lockwood et al., who found these four negative up to 20 mg/mL, and a validation study not read here (Kutscher et al., 2024). How often false positives happen when people test their own drugs, and whether a stimulant mixed with fentanyl changes the reading, were not measured; ways of preparing samples that authors proposed to avoid false positives were not tested. Certainty: very low. Status: replicated.
set.plain: Yes, sometimes. In laboratory tests, strong solutions of methamphetamine, MDMA, diphenhydramine (an allergy and sleep medicine) or lidocaine (a numbing medicine used as a cutting agent) made fentanyl strips read positive with no fentanyl present. It took thousands of times more of these drugs than the smallest amount of fentanyl the same strips could find. In one study of seized drugs, about 6 in 100 samples without fentanyl read positive. How often this happens when people test their own drugs is not known.
set.magnitude: Green et al.: specificity 98.1% (51/52) and 90.4% (47/52); 6/104 false positives (5.8%; specificity 94.2%, Wilson 95% CI 88.0–97.3%, editors' calculation). Lockwood et al. (weighed material, not pure drug; one strip per concentration): by eye above about 2 mg/mL; by image analysis diphenhydramine capsules 1, methamphetamine 1.5, MDMA 2, diphenhydramine tablets 2.5 mg/mL (about 0.10 and 0.25 mg/mL of diphenhydramine HCl, editors' calculation on the card); negative up to 20 mg/mL: cocaine and alprazolam, gabapentin and buprenorphine-naloxone products. Halifax et al. (pure standards; 2017 lots against 2021 lots): d-methamphetamine 5 against 10; MDMA 50 against 2.5–5; lidocaine 100 against 2.5 mg/mL; diphenhydramine 0.5–1 mg/mL on the 2021 lots, negative or invalid at 50 mg/mL and negative at 100 mg/mL on two of three lots, the 2017 lots positive at 100 mg/mL and not tested below 50 mg/mL; l-methamphetamine negative at 25 mg/mL; cocaine and ketamine negative at 25 mg/mL (2017 lots); levamisole none to 100 mg/mL (2021 lots). Bergh et al.: 12 non-fentanyl drugs negative at 100 and 1000 ng/mL on four brands; ascorbic acid 10 mg/mL or more positive on One Step only. Lowest false-positive concentration against the same strips' fentanyl limit (editors' calculation): 2,500 times (Halifax et al., 2021 lots) and about 40,000 times (Lockwood et al.). Second-hand specificity: 89.2–89.4% (via Kutscher et al.); 95.2% (Ti et al., 2020, via Klaire et al.). Klaire et al. (different samples, unconfirmed): crystal methamphetamine 73/265 (27.6% as printed; 27.5% by the counts) take-home against 5/97 (5.2%) on site; cocaine 16/93 (17.2%) against 1/92 (1.1%).
set.grade.domains.risk_of_bias.note: QUADAS-2 high in all four laboratory studies (study cards): Lockwood et al. chose materials that drug checkers suspected, of unreported purity, and read single strips against its own image-analysis threshold, set at a faint visible band; Halifax et al. used single pure analytes and tested old and new lots in separate rounds and over different concentration ranges; Green et al.'s reference was less sensitive than the strip, so some of its false positives may be true traces; Bergh et al. graded post hoc. Counted once.
set.grade.domains.inconsistency.note: Every study that tested methamphetamine, MDMA or diphenhydramine at mg/mL concentrations found false positives; Bergh et al.'s negatives were at 1 µg/mL or less, a thousand times lower, so they do not conflict. Thresholds differ by lot and by material (pure standard, seized or retail product) and are given as ranges; the unexplained diphenhydramine negatives at 50 and 100 mg/mL on the 2021 lots are reported.
set.grade.reasoning: Test-accuracy evidence starts high (METHODS §6.3, test accuracy); risk of bias, indirectness and imprecision each rate it down one level, so very low. Rated as worded: that strong solutions of these substances can turn the strip positive without fentanyl, at the stated concentrations, in laboratory conditions; the direction is consistent across independent laboratories (Lockwood et al.; Halifax et al.; Green et al.'s methamphetamine-only sample), so the status is replicated, while the thresholds themselves are uncertain. The scoping review relays Lockwood et al. and an unread study and is not counted; the second-hand specificity figures (Kutscher et al.; Klaire et al., citing Ti et al., 2020) come without their conditions and are not counted. Klaire et al. is observational, unconfirmed and on different samples; it qualifies the laboratory findings and is not counted as accuracy evidence.

set.statement: In laboratory tests of urine fentanyl test strips, mostly on single fentanyl analogues dissolved in water and compared with the known content of each solution, the strips reacted to most analogues tested, many of them only at concentrations well above those at which they detect fentanyl, and to a few not at all. With four brands and 28 analogues graded by the authors (no test band or a barely visible one counted as positive; no replicates reported), 21, 19, 15 and 22 analogues read positive at 1000 ng/mL and 24, 24, 21 and 24 at up to 10 000 ng/mL, but only 5, 5, 12 and 9 of the 23 measured at 100 ng/mL; under the makers' rule, which counts any visible test band as negative, fewer were positive (editors' recount on the study card: 20, 20, 19 and 21 of 28 at the highest concentrations). No brand detected alfentanil, despropionyl-2-fluorofentanyl or norcarfentanil; carfentanil read positive on no brand at 1000 ng/mL (a faint, weak or ambiguous test band on three brands, a solid band on the fourth), positive at 4000 ng/mL on three brands, and never on the fourth (Bergh et al., 2021). Five lots of one brand all detected 11 of the 13 analogues tested, carfentanil among them, with limits that differed between lots: carfentanil from 500 ng/mL on two lots obtained in 2017 but only from 10 000 ng/mL on two of three lots obtained in 2021; sufentanil was detected only by the 2017 lots, and only from 10 000 ng/mL; no lot detected alfentanil or the non-fentanyl opioid U-47700 at any concentration tested, up to 50 000 ng/mL (Halifax et al., 2024; per-lot values from the paper's figure). In four police-seized samples containing acetyl fentanyl or furanyl fentanyl, one brand read positive in all four, a set of four samples only (Green et al., 2020). Four analogues too dilute to show alone (10 ng/mL each) read positive when mixed, on the one brand tested (Bergh et al.). A scoping review relays, without concentrations or brands, that carfentanil, norcarfentanil and norfentanyl test negative (Kutscher et al., 2024, second-hand); in the two laboratory studies read here, carfentanil read negative at lower concentrations and positive at higher ones. The analogue panels were not chosen by how often each compound occurs in drug markets, and results came from pure compounds rather than mixtures. Certainty: very low. Status: replicated.
set.plain: In laboratory tests, fentanyl strips reacted to most drugs related to fentanyl, but some only in larger amounts than fentanyl itself, and a few never. Carfentanil showed up only in large amounts, never on one of four brands, and on two of three newer batches of another brand only in very large amounts. These were mostly pure drugs in water, tested by laboratory staff, with no repeat tests reported in the largest study.
set.magnitude: Bergh et al. (authors' rule): at 100 ng/mL Rapid Response 5, Rapid Self Test 5, One Step 12, Nal van Minden 9 of 23 measured; at 1000 ng/mL 21, 19, 15 and 22 of 28; cumulative to 10 000 ng/mL 24, 24, 21 and 24 of 28; makers' rule (editors' recount on the card): 1, 2, 11 and 4 of 23 at 100 ng/mL, 20, 20, 19 and 21 of 28 cumulative. Carfentanil: faint, weak or ambiguous (three brands) or negative (One Step) at 1000 ng/mL, positive at 4000 ng/mL on three brands. Halifax et al.: 11 analogues on all five lots; carfentanil lowest positive 500 ng/mL (2017 lots), 1000 ng/mL (lot 018) and 10 000 ng/mL (lots 188 and 196); sufentanil on 2017 lots only, from 10 000 ng/mL; alfentanil and U-47700 not detected up to 50 000 ng/mL. Green et al.: 4 of 4 seized analogue samples positive.
set.grade.domains.inconsistency.note: The two laboratories agree on the pattern (most analogues detected, alfentanil never, carfentanil only at higher concentrations, on some lots only from 10 000 ng/mL); the review's statement that carfentanil tests negative is second-hand, gives no concentrations and is not counted.
set.grade.domains.imprecision.note: Bergh et al. report no replicates for any compound and concentration, and its table and figure grade the same fentanyl result differently; Halifax et al. used duplicates with one consensus reading per step, and two of its series are non-monotone; Green et al.'s analogue set had four samples.

set.statement: In laboratory tests, fentanyl test strips of different brands, production lots and ages did not perform the same, compared with the known content of prepared solutions. Lots: in one laboratory, two lots of one brand (BTNX Rapid Response, urine cut-off 20 ng/mL) obtained in 2017 detected fentanyl in water down to 20 ng/mL, while three lots obtained in 2021 detected it only down to 200 ng/mL, ten times higher, and in urine, the strips' intended use, down to 50–100 ng/mL; the 2021 lots also gave false positives with lidocaine and MDMA at concentrations 10 to 40 times lower than the 2017 lots, with d-methamphetamine at a twofold higher one (editors' calculation), and with diphenhydramine from 0.5–1 mg/mL, a range in which the 2017 lots were not tested. The two sets were tested in separate rounds (2017 and 2022), with storage and expiry not reported, so lot, storage and testing round cannot be separated (Halifax et al., 2024). Brands: on the same solutions, four brands detected 5 to 12 of the 23 analogues measured at 100 ng/mL (editors' count); one brand (One Step), which detected the most of them at 100 ng/mL, read negative for carfentanil, sufentanil and benzodioxolefentanyl at every concentration, which the other three detected at higher concentrations, and it alone gave false positives with ascorbic acid at 10 mg/mL or more (Bergh et al., 2021). Heat and age: strips with a listed cut-off of 200 ng/mL detected 500 ng/mL whether or not they had been kept unopened at 55 °C for two weeks; strips with a listed cut-off of 20 ng/mL, more than four years past expiry and kept in laboratory conditions, detected 250 ng/mL, but no in-date strips of that kind were tested (the in-date strips tested, listed at 200 ng/mL, were apparently a different product or version), so the effect of age cannot be separated from the product (Sisco et al., 2024b; apparently one lot each, triplicates). In another laboratory, diphenhydramine solutions tested at 4 °C read positive on every strip at all three concentrations tried, while at 25 and 40 °C the readings followed concentration; no drug-free (water) blank or fentanyl solution was reported at 4 °C (Lockwood et al., 2021). How strips perform after storage as people keep them, after longer heat, or across many lots and brands was not measured. Certainty: very low. Status: replicated.
set.plain: No. In laboratory tests, batches of one brand bought in 2021 needed ten times more fentanyl to show it than batches bought in 2017, and four brands differed in which related drugs they picked up. Two weeks of heat did not change one kind of strip. Strips more than four years out of date still worked but needed more fentanyl than their label said; no new strips of the same kind were tested to compare. Why batches differed could not be worked out from these studies.
set.magnitude: Halifax et al.: fentanyl in water 20 ng/mL (2017 lots) against 200 ng/mL (2021 lots); in urine 50 and 100 ng/mL (2021 lots); false-positive thresholds 2017 against 2021 lots: d-methamphetamine 5 against 10, MDMA 50 against 2.5–5, lidocaine 100 against 2.5 mg/mL; diphenhydramine 0.5–1 mg/mL on the 2021 lots, not comparable with the 2017 lots, which were tested only at 50 mg/mL and above (positive at 100). Bergh et al.: analogues at 100 ng/mL 5, 5, 12 and 9 of 23 measured by brand (editors' count); One Step negative for carfentanil, sufentanil and benzodioxolefentanyl at all concentrations; ascorbic acid false positives on One Step only. Sisco et al. (2024b): fentanyl strips 0.5 µg/mL heated or not (listed 0.2 µg/mL); expired fentanyl strips of another kind 0.25 µg/mL (listed 0.02 µg/mL); expired methamphetamine strips 5 against 1 µg/mL; expired cocaine strips unchanged at 2.5 µg/mL. Lockwood et al.: at 4 °C all diphenhydramine strips positive at 4, 2 and 1 mg/mL.
set.grade.domains.risk_of_bias.note: QUADAS-2 high for Halifax et al. (lot comparison confounded with testing round and unreported storage, and the 2017 lots tested over narrower concentration ranges) and Bergh et al. (post hoc, unblinded grading); Sisco et al. (2024b), re-filed as test-accuracy with QUADAS-2 in this round (high), compared expired strips with their labels rather than with fresh strips of the same kind; Lockwood et al.'s cold result had no drug-free cold blank.
set.grade.domains.indirectness.note: Laboratory solutions read by trained staff; one brand's lots, four brands, and apparently one lot each for heat and expiry; storage as people keep strips was not studied.
set.grade.domains.imprecision.note: Duplicate strips per concentration (Halifax et al.), no replicates reported (Bergh et al.) and triplicates (Sisco et al., 2024b) at steps two- to fivefold apart, so differences of one step may be test-to-test variation; no repeatability was measured.
set.grade.reasoning: Test-accuracy evidence starts high; one level each for risk of bias, indirectness and imprecision gives very low. Rated as worded: that strips differed between brands, lots and ages in laboratory tests, not why they differed. Status replicated: independent laboratories found differences between brands (Bergh et al.) and between lots (Halifax et al.); the heat and expiry findings come from one laboratory study (Sisco et al., 2024b, re-filed as test-accuracy in this round).

evidence_set: False-positive thresholds, 2017 lots against 2021 lots: d-methamphetamine 5 against 10 mg/mL, MDMA 50 against 2.5–5, lidocaine 100 against 2.5, diphenhydramine 100 against 0.5–1 mg/mL. Editors' calculation on the study card: 10- to 20-fold lower for MDMA, 40-fold for lidocaine and 2-fold higher for d-methamphetamine.

Diphenhydramine tablets and capsules at 4, 2 and 1 mg/mL were tested at 4, 25 and 40 °C: at 25 and 40 °C the readings followed concentration, but at 4 °C every strip showed only the control band (a positive reading); no drug-free (water) blank or fentanyl solution was reported at 4 °C, and the authors generalize from this single cold condition.

set.statement: In laboratory tests of the first commercial nitazene test strip (BTNX Rapid Response; maker's cut-off 2000 ng/mL isotonitazene) on pure nitazene standards in water and on nearly pure powders from drug-market monitoring, compared with known content, the strips detected most nitazenes tested but missed six of the seven desnitazenes tested and three other analogues. Read from photographs by two blinded raters and by image analysis, isotonitazene read positive in all six replicates from 3000 ng/mL with one lot and 2000 ng/mL with another, obtained about four months apart. With one lot and one strip per concentration, 24 of 33 nitazene analogues read positive at 9000 ng/mL or less; nine did not at 9000 ng/mL: six desnitazenes, which lack the 5-nitro group (among them metodesnitazene and etodesnitazene), 5-aminoisotonitazene and two analogues with a longer link between the rings; the seventh desnitazene tested, 5-methyl etodesnitazene, was detected. Six powders obtained in Belgian drug-market monitoring, each estimated as more than 90% one nitazene, all read positive at about 1 and 0.1 mg/mL (6 of 6; editors' Wilson 95% CI 61.0–100%) (De Vrieze et al., 2024). In a second laboratory, the strips detected metonitazene from 1 µg/mL and N-piperidinyl etonitazene and protonitazene from 5 µg/mL (ten strips per level), and reacted to none of 76 other drugs, cutting agents and other compounds at two concentrations (Sisco et al., 2024b). No study read tested nitazene-free street samples or mixtures in which a nitazene is a small part of heroin, other opioids or stimulants, so how often the strips miss nitazenes or give false positives in real samples is unknown; preliminary street-sample figures cited from the maker's material (12 samples) are unpublished. The first study's authors write that a negative result does not mean a sample is free of nitazenes or safe, and that a positive one does not show which nitazene is present or how much. Certainty: very low. Status: replicated.
set.plain: In laboratory tests, nitazene test strips showed most nitazenes (24 of 33 tested) and all six nearly pure powders from the drug market. They missed most desnitazenes, a group of nitazenes, even in large amounts. Only pure drugs were tested, so how well they work on mixed street drugs is not known.
set.population: Nitazene reference standards in water (33 analogues in one laboratory, three in another), six nearly pure nitazene powders from Belgian drug-market monitoring, and 76 other drugs, cutting agents and other compounds
set.magnitude: De Vrieze et al.: isotonitazene limit (all six replicates positive) 3000 ng/mL (lot A) and 2000 ng/mL (lot B), the same by visual and image-analysis scoring; analogues (lot B, single strips) 24 of 33 positive at 9000 ng/mL or less (visually 16 at 1000 and 3000 ng/mL, 7 at 3000 ng/mL only, 1 at 9000 ng/mL only, by the text), 9 not detected at 9000 ng/mL (six of seven desnitazenes, 5-aminoisotonitazene, two ethylene-linker analogues); powders 6 of 6 positive at both concentrations (Wilson 95% CI 61.0–100%, editors' calculation on the card). Sisco et al. (2024b): limits 1 µg/mL (metonitazene) and 5 µg/mL (N-piperidinyl etonitazene, protonitazene); no reaction with 76 non-nitazene compounds at 0.01 and 0.5 or 1 mg/mL.
set.grade.domains.risk_of_bias.note: QUADAS-2 high for De Vrieze et al. (study card: pure positives and blank negatives, a two-gate design that can overstate accuracy, though raters were blinded and replicated) and for Sisco et al. (2024b), re-filed as test-accuracy with QUADAS-2 in this round (pure standards at chosen concentrations, readers probably aware of the content).

evidence_set: Six powders obtained earlier in routine drug-market monitoring by the Belgian Early Warning System on Drugs (metonitazene, protonitazene, isotonitazene, butonitazene and two N-pyrrolidino etonitazene samples), not described as seized, each with the nitazene as the major compound at an estimated purity above 90% by LC-QTOF-MS, were each tested once at about 1 mg/mL and once at a tenfold lower concentration, with some powder undissolved: all readings were positive by both scoring methods, and the blank was negative. Editors' calculation on the study card: 6 of 6, Wilson 95% CI 61.0–100%.
Materials and methods › Materials, 1st paragraph; Materials and methods › Methods › Testing of authentic powder samples, 1st paragraph; Results › Testing of authentic powder samples, 1st paragraph

set.statement: In residue samples swabbed from used drug equipment and in pure xylazine solutions, one production lot of BTNX xylazine test strips read in a laboratory, compared with quantitative GC-MS/MS or known content, read positive in nearly all residue samples with at least the strip's listed amount of xylazine, read positive on every strip in pure solutions only from 2.5 times that amount, and often missed smaller amounts. Of 100 residue samples from syringes, bags and pill bottles collected in two US states, the strips read positive in 37 of 38 with xylazine at or above the listed 1 µg/mL cut-off (sensitivity 97.4%; editors' Wilson 95% CI 86.5–99.5%; the one miss had 2 µg/mL) and in none of 34 without xylazine (one faint; specificity 100%; 89.8–100%), but in only 6 of 28 with less xylazine, so 43 of all 66 xylazine-containing samples read positive (65%; 53–76%; editors' calculation). In pure solutions, all 15 strips per level read positive from 2.5 µg/mL; at the listed 1 µg/mL cut-off 3 of 15 were positive and 12 showed a faint test band, counted as negative. Of 76 other compounds tested at 100 µg/mL with two strips each, only lidocaine, a common cutting agent, read positive; the veterinary sedative medetomidine and the α2-agonists clonidine, detomidine, romifidine and tizanidine did not at that concentration, the only one tested, so at that level these strips would not show them; higher concentrations, as from dissolved powders, were not tested (Sisco et al., 2024a). A later version of the strip with a different antibody, tested in water in the same first author's laboratory, detected 1 µg/mL, did not react to lidocaine, levamisole, ketamine or medetomidine, reacted to brimonidine, clonidine, romifidine and tizanidine at high concentrations, and after two weeks unopened at 55 °C needed 10 µg/mL (Sisco et al., 2024b). Powders and pills dissolved as people do, other lots and brands, and reading outside a laboratory were not tested. Certainty: low. Status: replicated by the same team.
set.plain: In a laboratory, xylazine test strips showed xylazine in 37 of 38 residue samples that had at least the amount the strip is made to find, and in none of 34 without it. With smaller amounts they often missed it, and in pure water every strip read positive only at 2.5 times that amount. At the one amount tested, they did not react to medetomidine, a similar animal sedative. One batch of strips was tested, on residues wiped from used equipment rather than on powders.
set.magnitude: Sisco et al. (2024a), residues: 1 µg/mL or more 37/38 positive (97.4%; Wilson 86.5–99.5%; the one miss at 2 µg/mL); none detected 0/34 positive, 1 faint (specificity 100%; 89.8–100%); below 1 µg/mL 6/28 positive, 10 faint, 12 negative; all xylazine-containing samples 43/66 positive (65%; 53–76%) (editors' calculations on the card). Pure xylazine: 15/15 positive at 2.5 µg/mL and above; 3/15 at 1 µg/mL (12 faint); 7/15 at 0.5 µg/mL (8 faint); 0/15 at 0.1 µg/mL. Cross-reactivity at 100 µg/mL only: lidocaine alone of 76 other compounds. Sisco et al. (2024b), newer version: limit 1 µg/mL; brimonidine, clonidine, romifidine and tizanidine cross-reacted at high concentrations; heated strips needed 10 µg/mL.
set.grade.reasoning: Test-accuracy evidence on real residues against quantitative GC-MS/MS starts high; one level each for risk of bias and indirectness gives low. Rated as worded. The two studies share their first author and laboratory and test different versions of the strip, so the status is replicated by the same team; the newer version rests on one laboratory study in pure solutions (Sisco et al., 2024b, re-filed as test-accuracy with QUADAS-2 in this round).

change: Review and adjudication, drug checking round: The opening no longer says the strips detected xylazine 'reliably' from the listed amount: they read positive in 37 of 38 residues at or above it (the miss at 2 µg/mL), but in pure solutions every strip read positive only from 2.5 µg/mL, and the authors themselves describe consistent detection above 2 µg/mL (second reader 142, confirmed on pp. 945–946 and Table 2). The statement that the strips would not show medetomidine and other α2-agonists is limited to the one concentration tested (100 µg/mL), as the authors' limitations allow (second reader 142). Reasoning updated for the re-filing of sc_sisco_2024b. Anchor 3 now says strips 'may be used' by dissolving powder, as the source does, instead of 'people dissolve' (targeted check by AI reader 142, note; wording only, no new number). No new anchor. Certainty unchanged (low). AI reader 148 (adjudicator), 27 October 2026; log data/verification/dc-2026-10-26/adjudication/148_log.json.

set.statement: In drug-checking samples brought to eight harm-reduction sites in Vancouver and Surrey between October 2018 and January 2020, benzodiazepine urine test strips (BTNX Rapid Response, made to detect urine metabolites of common benzodiazepines) read at the sites, after infrared spectroscopy of the same sample and with one combined result recorded, compared with confirmatory laboratory tests on a convenience subset of 153 samples from five of the sites, partly chosen because of suspected benzodiazepine overdose, missed many of the newer benzodiazepines not sold as medicines (NPS benzodiazepines) and also gave false positives. The strips read positive in 15 of 24 samples that contained an NPS benzodiazepine (62.5%; editors' Wilson 95% CI 42.7–78.8%): in 7 of 8 when flualprazolam, flubromazolam or flubromazepam was present, but in 8 of 16 when etizolam was the only one (50%). They also read positive in 20 of 129 samples in which no NPS benzodiazepine was found (15.5%; 10.3–22.7%), and what made those react was not reported. Infrared spectroscopy (FTIR), used beside the strips, found 2 of the 24. The strips detected the prescribed benzodiazepines alprazolam and temazepam in all six samples that held only these (Laing et al., 2021). In pure solutions, the same maker's benzodiazepine strip detected diazepam and alprazolam from 0.1 µg/mL and bromazolam and flubromazepam from 0.25 µg/mL, but did not react to etizolam at any concentration tried from 0.01 to 0.5 mg/mL, 40 times or more the concentrations at which it detected the others (editors' calculation) (Sisco et al., 2024b). A report relayed second-hand by Laing et al. found that similar strips detected etizolam at a higher minimum concentration than other NPS benzodiazepines, still within the range useful for drug checking (Shapiro et al., 2020), so the sources disagree on whether these strips react to etizolam at all; differences in lots or test conditions may explain it, but this was not shown. Only 159 of 1368 strip-tested samples had laboratory confirmation, the two confirmatory laboratories disagreed on 2 of 7 positive samples tested at both, etizolam is reported to dissolve poorly in water, and targeted laboratory methods may miss the newest compounds; none of the 24 samples was expected by the person to contain an NPS benzodiazepine, and 17 of them also contained fentanyl. Certainty: very low. Status: replicated.
set.plain: Often not. At one drug-checking service, benzodiazepine strips missed 9 of 24 samples that held a newer benzodiazepine, and half of the samples with etizolam alone. They also read positive in about 16 in 100 samples with none. In a laboratory, the same maker's strip never reacted to pure etizolam, though an earlier report said similar strips could pick it up in larger amounts. Few samples were checked by a laboratory, and many were chosen after suspected overdoses.
set.exposure: BTNX benzodiazepine urine test strips (oxazepam calibrator, cut-off 300 ng/mL) used on dissolved drug at the sites after FTIR of the same sample, with one combined result recorded; the same maker's strip in pure solutions
set.magnitude: Laing et al. (153 samples with point-of-care and confirmatory results; 6 with only typical benzodiazepines removed): strips 15/24 NPS-benzodiazepine samples positive (62.5%; Wilson 42.7–78.8%, editors' calculation), false-negative rate 37.5%; 20/129 negatives positive (15.5%; 10.3–22.7%), specificity 84.5% (editors' calculation); 87.5% (n = 8) with flualprazolam, flubromazolam or flubromazepam; 50.0% (n = 16; 28.0–72.0%) with etizolam alone; FTIR 2/24 (false-negative rate 91.7%), false-positive rate 3.9%; either method 17/24 detected, 23 false positives. Sisco et al. (2024b): limits 0.1 µg/mL (diazepam, alprazolam) and 0.25 µg/mL (bromazolam, flubromazepam); etizolam negative from 0.01 to 0.5 mg/mL, 40 to 100 times or more those limits (editors' calculation). Second-hand (Shapiro et al., 2020, via Laing et al.): similar strips detected etizolam at a higher minimum concentration than flualprazolam and flubromazolam.
set.grade.domains.risk_of_bias.note: Laing et al. compares strips with confirmatory tests inside programme data (filed cross-sectional with JBI-prevalence, high, on the card) and is treated as accuracy evidence with high risk of bias: only 159 of 1368 point-of-care-tested samples were verified, chosen for convenience and partly because of suspected benzodiazepine overdose; the strip was read after FTIR of the same sample with one combined result recorded; the targeted two-laboratory reference disagreed on 2 of 7 duplicate samples; strip lots were not reported. The biases can run in either direction; very serious, two levels.
set.grade.domains.inconsistency.note: Both primary studies find etizolam poorly detected; the difference in degree (half of etizolam-only samples positive in programme data, never in pure solution) may reflect other reacting compounds, untargeted benzodiazepines, lots or conditions, and is reported in the claim; the second-hand report that similar strips detected etizolam at higher concentrations is not counted, so not rated down.
set.grade.domains.indirectness.note: Strips read at harm-reduction sites in one urban area (2018 to 2020) and pure solutions in a laboratory; one brand, made for urine.
set.grade.reasoning: Test-accuracy evidence starts high; Laing et al.'s agreement figures are accuracy evidence with high risk of bias (METHODS §6.3), so two levels for risk of bias and one each for indirectness and imprecision take it to the floor of very low. Rated as worded. Status replicated: independent teams (British Columbia; NIST) both found etizolam poorly detected; Sisco et al. (2024b) is re-filed as test-accuracy with QUADAS-2 in this round; the Shapiro et al. report is second-hand and not counted.

Second-hand: a report on similar strips (Shapiro et al., 2020) concluded that flualprazolam and flubromazolam were detected at concentrations similar to alprazolam, and etizolam at a higher minimum concentration that was still within the range useful for drug checking; the authors cite it as recent evidence of cross-reactivity supporting point-of-care use. The report was not read.

set.statement: In one laboratory study of a three-reagent colour kit for ecstasy (Marquis, Mecke and Simon's reagents; two identical DanceSafe kits bought online, without lot numbers), compared with GC-MS or the known identity of the drugs, readings by experienced analysts matched whether MDMA was present, readings by two testers new to the kit did not, and a positive reading never showed a second drug. Three experienced analysts using the kit's instructions and colour charts read all 35 seized samples that contained MDMA as positive and the four without MDMA as negative, except that one analyst read one of the four, which held no identifiable drug, as weakly positive (editors' Wilson 95% CI 90.1–100% for 35 of 35, 51.0–100% for 4 of 4); the seven MDMA samples that also held caffeine, ephedrine, amphetamine, diazepam or PMMA read like the rest. Two testers trained in pharmacology but new to the kit, given eight samples of known drugs and only the kit's leaflet, diverged: one read both MDMA samples as negative, the other read codeine, dihydrocodeine, dextromethorphan and morphine as MDMA or MDMA-like; together 2 of 4 MDMA readings were positive and 7 of 12 non-MDMA readings negative, and with the Marquis reagent alone 10 of the 12 non-MDMA readings were positive (Murray et al., 2003). A laboratory comparison from an unpublished thesis, known only from a narrative review (156 amnesty-bin samples, Marquis read by laboratory staff before GC-MS), found the MDMA colour (purple, blue or black) in all 53 samples with MDMA-like substances and in no others, but 14 other samples gave a purple/violet reading that staff filed as the opiate colour, and 43 presumptive colour readings in all had no matching drug (editors' sum); its table holds 187 entries for 156 samples (Winstock et al., 2001). Two narrative reviews add, second-hand, that colour tests are presumptive, that other substances react too (the Marquis reagent also with aspirin and sugar) and that more than one drug or tablet dyes can change the result (Philp & Fu, 2018; Winstock et al., 2001); one adds that MDMA, MDEA and MDA give similar colours and that, read by eye, the tests show nothing about a pill's strength (Winstock et al., 2001). No sample contained PMA, MDA or methamphetamine, and the kit and drug market were those of the early 2000s. Certainty: very low. Status: single study.
set.plain: In one laboratory study from 2003, experts reading a three-reagent colour kit got MDMA right in all 35 samples that had it, and nearly always right in the 4 without it. But the colour looked the same when another drug was mixed in, and two people new to the kit made many mistakes, calling several other drugs MDMA. Read by eye, colour tests do not show how much MDMA is in a pill.
set.magnitude: Murray et al. Part I (experienced analysts, three reagents): 35/35 MDMA samples positive (Wilson 90.1–100%, editors' calculation); 4/4 non-MDMA negative for two analysts (51.0–100%), 3/4 for the third (one weak positive); 7 samples with a second drug read like MDMA alone. Part II (two novices, 8 known drugs, three reagents): sensitivity 2/4 (50%), specificity 7/12 (58%), positive and negative predictive values 2/7 and 7/9 (printed 28% and 77%); Novice A 0/2 MDMA detected and 5/6 others negative, Novice B 2/2 and 2/6; Marquis alone 10 false positives in 12 non-MDMA readings and 2 false negatives. Winstock et al. (second-hand, Murphy 1999): purple/blue/black 53/53 MDMA-like and 0 others; orange/brown 47 amphetamine samples and 21 without; yellow/green 8 and purple/violet 14 with no matching GC-MS class (43 in all, editors' sum); 187 cell entries for n = 156.
set.grade.domains.indirectness.note: A 2003 kit read in a laboratory by analysts who had practised and agreed colour names beforehand (study card), seized samples of the early 2000s with no PMA, MDA or methamphetamine, and newer substances untested; the novice part used legitimate medicines rather than street drugs.

set.statement: In British Columbia in 2019, take-home testing by people who use drugs (strips from ten harm-reduction sites, used at home on 55 in 100 result sheets, in alleys and streets on 22 and at supervised consumption or overdose prevention sites on 29, more than one setting possible; 218 people returning 336 result sheets) compared with on-site testing of other samples by trained staff at the same sites in the same four months was associated with a similar share of fentanyl-positive results for opioid samples and a much larger share for stimulant samples. Opioids: 994 of 1105 take-home results positive (90.0%) against 591 of 663 on site (89.1%), a difference of 0.8 percentage points (95% CI −2.3 to 3.9) within the pre-set equivalence margin of ±5 points. Crystal methamphetamine: 73 of 265 (27.6% as printed) against 5 of 97 (5.2%); cocaine: 16 of 93 (17.2%) against 1 of 92 (1.1%); the study was not powered for these. By design no sample was tested both ways, and nothing was confirmed in a laboratory, so these are shares of positive results, not accuracy; the authors nonetheless conclude that people can use the strips accurately with minimal training, and think the stimulant excess mostly reflects false positives from how samples were prepared, which was not tested (Klaire et al., 2022). Results were self-reported, about 6 in 10 sheets were filled in from memory at return (by the paper's Table 3; its text gives the reverse), the number of kits handed out and not returned is unknown, and similar shares near 90% can hide reading errors in both directions. A scoping review relays from other studies that 3% to almost 34% of people had difficulty interpreting results and that some believed the line's strength showed how strong the fentanyl was (Kutscher et al., 2024, second-hand; its figure of positives five times more frequent at home is this same study and holds only for crystal methamphetamine); a 2018 commentary relays a preliminary study, with design and testers not stated, in which 7 of 70 samples gave erroneous or invalid results (McGowan et al., 2018, second-hand); and in a laboratory study of a colour kit, two testers new to it misread known drugs in both directions (Murray et al., 2003). Certainty: very low. Status: single study.
set.plain: When people tested their own drugs with strips they took home (used at home a little over half the time), the share of opioid samples showing fentanyl was about the same as when staff tested other samples on site (90 against 89 in 100). For crystal meth and cocaine, take-home tests showed fentanyl far more often (28 against 5 in 100 for meth), which the authors think were mostly false positives. No laboratory checked which results were right, and the two groups tested different samples.
set.magnitude: Opioids: take-home 994/1105 (90.0%) against on-site 591/663 (89.1%); difference 0.8 points (95% CI −2.3 to 3.9), equivalent within ±5 (p = 0.00275). Crystal methamphetamine 73/265 (27.6% as printed; 27.5% by the counts, editors' calculation) against 5/97 (5.2%), difference 22.4 (14.8 to 30.1); cocaine 16/93 (17.2%) against 1/92 (1.1%), difference 16.1 (7.1 to 25.1). Settings of take-home use (sheets, more than one possible): home 184 (54.8%), alleys and streets 74 (22.0%), supervised sites 97 (28.9%). Second-hand: difficulty interpreting results 3% to almost 34% (Kutscher et al.); its 'five times more frequent at home' matches this study's crystal methamphetamine figures only (27.6% against 5.2%, 5.3-fold; cocaine about 16-fold; opioids equal; editors' calculation); 7 of 70 erroneous or invalid results in a preliminary study (McGowan et al.).
set.grade.domains.indirectness.note: Shares of positive results stand in for accuracy; take-home strips were used at home on only a little over half of the sheets; one province in 2019, one brand.
set.grade.reasoning: Observational evidence starts low; risk of bias, indirectness and imprecision each rate it down, to the floor of very low. Rated as worded: agreement of shares of positive results between people using take-home strips and staff testing on site, not the accuracy of home testing, which no study read measured; whether home testing changes behaviour is a separate question. Status single study: the review's 'five times' figure is the same study, and Murray et al. concerns a colour kit in a laboratory and only qualifies.

set.statement: In the studies read, a test that showed one drug did not show what else was in the sample or, read by eye, how much drug it held, and no study measured whether a negative result means a sample is less risky. A colour kit read by experienced analysts gave the same positive MDMA reading for seven samples that also held caffeine, ephedrine, amphetamine, diazepam or PMMA as for samples of MDMA alone (Murray et al., 2003). In drug-checking samples in the Vancouver area, 24 of 159 contained a newer benzodiazepine that the person had not expected (most expected fentanyl), 17 of them also held fentanyl, and infrared spectroscopy alone, which can identify several components, listed fentanyl in only 3 of those 17 and a benzodiazepine in 2 of the 24 (editors' count from the paper's table; Laing et al., 2021). Each strip type reacts to one drug or family and missed related drugs in laboratory tests: xylazine strips did not react to medetomidine or several other sedatives at the concentration tested (Sisco et al., 2024a), and nitazene, fentanyl and benzodiazepine strips missed some nitazenes, fentanyl analogues and etizolam (see the answers on each strip). Fentanyl strips are built to show presence only, not concentration, purity or which analogue (Green et al., 2020); in pure solutions the test band became fainter as the fentanyl concentration rose, but the makers' rule reads only whether a band is there (Bergh et al., 2021), no study read tested whether a line's strength shows how much drug a sample holds, and a scoping review lists that belief among mistaken ones (Kutscher et al., 2024, second-hand). The authors of the nitazene study state that a negative result does not mean a sample is safe and that a positive one gives no amount (De Vrieze et al., 2024); the xylazine study's authors, that sedatives the strips miss could give a false sense of safety (Sisco et al., 2024a); and a critique, that colour tests show neither many harmful substances nor a pill's strength (Winstock et al., 2001); these are their conclusions, not tested findings. Certainty: very low. Status: replicated.
set.magnitude: Murray et al.: 7 of 35 MDMA samples held a second drug, all read like MDMA alone. Laing et al.: 24/159 samples held an NPS benzodiazepine (15.1%), none expected; 17 of 24 also held fentanyl; FTIR alone listed fentanyl in 3 of those 17 and an NPS benzodiazepine in 2 of 24 (editors' count from Table 2). Sisco et al. (2024a): medetomidine and the other α2-agonists in the panel did not react at the one concentration tested. Amount: no study read tested whether strips or colour tests read by eye estimate amount.
